title: Regular Expression Matching
description: Full-string match of a pattern built from literals, dot and star.
statement:
A validation service must decide whether an entire identifier matches a supplied pattern, without any partial matches and without regular-expression syntax beyond two operators.

You are given a string `s` and a pattern `p`. The pattern is built from three kinds of element:

- a lowercase letter, which matches that letter exactly;
- `.`, which matches any single character;
- `*`, which applies to the element before it and means **zero or more** repetitions of that element (for example `a*` matches `aaa`, `a` or nothing at all).

Report `true` only when the pattern matches the **whole** string - a pattern that covers just a prefix is a failure. A pattern that a regular-expression engine would reject (for instance a leading `*`) never matches.

The natural solution is dynamic programming over prefixes, in which each cell records whether one prefix of the string matches one prefix of the pattern, and a star collapses to two cases: skip the starred element, or consume one character and stay on the same pattern position.
inputFormat:
The input is read from standard input as exactly two lines:

1. Line 1: the string `s` - lowercase ASCII letters only, never empty (`1 <= length <= 200`).
2. Line 2: the pattern `p` - a non-empty sequence of lowercase letters, `.` and `*` (`1 <= length <= 200`). A pattern may begin with `*` or contain `**`, and such a pattern never matches. Read each line in full.
outputFormat: Print a single line containing the lowercase word `true` if `p` matches the entire string `s`, otherwise the lowercase word `false`.
constraints: s contains lowercase ASCII letters only
p contains lowercase ASCII letters, `.` and `*` only
The match must cover the whole string; partial matches do not count
notes: `*` always follows a character, and zero repetitions is always allowed - so `a*` matches the empty contribution, and `ab*` matches `a`. Use `re.fullmatch` and `re.match` with an explicit end anchor carefully: Python's `re` also understands operators the problem does not define, so if your language's engine supports `+`, `?`, `[]` or `()`, do not let them leak into the interpretation. A pattern beginning with `*` is invalid and never matches.

testCases.explanation:
Step 1: the pattern is one literal `a`, so it can match a string of length 1 only.
Step 2: `s` has length 2.
Step 3: there is no way for one literal to consume two characters, and the pattern does not cover the whole string.
Step 4: the full match fails, so print `false`.

Step 1: `a*` matches zero or more repetitions of the character `a`.
Step 2: two repetitions consume the whole string, so the match covers all of `s`.
Step 3: the match succeeds.
Step 4: print `true`.

Step 1: `.` matches any single character and `*` allows zero or more of them.
Step 2: two repetitions of `.` consume `a` and `b`.
Step 3: the pattern covers the entire string, so the match succeeds.
Step 4: print `true`.
